Figure 1B: is the increase from 158 to 182 red sites unusual within the randomization blocks?¶

This notebook reconstructs Figure 1B of Karbacher et al. and tests the after-minus-before increase of +24 using participant reassignment.

Update recorded on 6 November 2026: Max Storz confirmed 0 = vegan, 1 = meat-rich and supplied explicit randomization-block membership. The workbook matches all 48 participants, and every diet assignment agrees with the numeric codes already used. The current run shuffles within these blocks, preserving each block's observed diet counts. See the allocation note and validated allocation table.

The four visit corrections for donors 5 and 8 remain in place, giving 158 before and 182 after, matching the published counts. See the visit-correction note. Earlier unrestricted runs are preserved and compared below.

Scope: a conditional within-block permutation test for the analyzed subset. Its validity requires joint exchangeability within the supplied blocks after selection into this subset. The full recruitment and replacement mechanism is not reconstructed.

We keep methylation measurements fixed, use the same participant assignment across both visits and every CpG, refit limma, and count sites passing the same thresholds. Run All checks saved results; it does not perform thousands of new fits. The README documents the complete pipeline.

Loaded 812,934 CpGs, 48 participants, and a saved run of 9,999 permutations.

1. Observed red-site counts¶

A site is red when it meets both original rules: limma raw two-sided $p < 0.05$ and $|\Delta M| > 0.5$. Every shuffled analysis uses these same rules. These are counts of thresholded CpGs, rather than genome-wide discoveries after multiple-testing correction. The effect scale and candidate model are explained below.

2. Test the change: after minus before¶

At each visit $v$, count sites passing the original red-site rule:

$$C_v = \sum_{j=1}^{812934} \mathbf{1}\{p^{\mathrm{limma}}_{j,v}<0.05 \;\mathrm{and}\;|\Delta M_{j,v}|>0.5\}.$$

Our statistic is the signed count change:

$$D = C_{\mathrm{after}}-C_{\mathrm{before}},\qquad D_{\mathrm{observed}}=182-158=24.$$

The saved simulation refitted the corrected data 9,999 times, using seed 70899:

  1. Keep all methylation measurements fixed.
  2. Shuffle diet labels within each supplied randomization block, preserving its observed diet totals. Overall group sizes remain 24/24; participant 57 stays fixed because only one member of that replacement block is included.
  3. Apply the same assignment to both visits and every CpG. Each person's before/after pair stays together, and the relationships between CpGs are preserved.
  4. Refit the same four group-by-visit means and re-estimate limma's empirical Bayes variance prior. Apply exactly the same raw-p and effect thresholds.
  5. Record the before and after red-site counts for that assignment.

We now subtract those counts within each saved row to obtain $D_b$. No new model fits are needed. We do not independently shuffle visits or mix counts from different assignments. To ask whether the observed increase is unusually large, use

$$p_{\mathrm{increase}} =\frac{1+\#\{D_b\ge24\}}{9999+1}.$$

This is a one-sided upper-tail test, including ties. The added 1 accounts for the observed assignment in the Monte Carlo calculation. The site-level limma p-values inside the red-site rule remain two-sided. This answers the question about an increase; testing unusually large changes in either direction would require a two-sided statistic.

The histogram is zoomed to changes between −200 and 200; its footnote gives the number outside this view. All 9,999 changes contribute to the p-value, regardless of the displayed range. The red line marks +24; dark bars show increases of +24 or more. Each shuffle uses its own baseline count, so this is not conditional on starting at exactly 158 and is not the probability of the exact pair 158 → 182. The middle 95% range describes shuffled changes, not a confidence interval for a diet effect.

Allocation assumption: whole participant profiles must be exchangeable within blocks under the null, conditional on the analyzed subset and its observed block-specific diet counts. Four original blocks had planned size 13; two replacement blocks had planned size 4. The included counts are 10, 10, 13, 11, 3 and 1, respectively. We use the supplied membership rather than infer blocks from sorted IDs.

The workbook does not establish the recruitment, replacement and missingness mechanism for participants outside this subset. The restriction therefore supports a conditional test, subject to the subset-selection assumption, rather than reconstruction of the full trial's unconditional allocation process. See the allocation note and exchangeability reference.

null_counts = pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv")
B = len(null_counts)
assert B == run["repetitions"]
# Subtract within each assignment: before and after share the same participant grouping.
changes = null_counts["after"] - null_counts["before"]
observed_change = int(summary.loc["after", "highlighted"] - summary.loc["before", "highlighted"])
extreme_changes = int((changes >= observed_change).sum())
change_p = (1 + extreme_changes) / (B + 1)

# Independently check the saved summary and paired export before displaying them.
saved_changes = pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_changes.csv")
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes["shuffle"], np.arange(1, B+1))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes[["before", "after"]], null_counts[["before", "after"]])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(saved_changes["change"], changes)
saved_change_test = pd.read_csv(OUT / "change_test_summary.csv").iloc[0]
assert observed_change == saved_change_test.observed_change
assert extreme_changes == saved_change_test.shuffles_ge_observed
assert np.isclose(change_p, saved_change_test.change_p_upper)

change_results = pd.DataFrame([{
    "Observed change": observed_change,
    "Shuffle median change": changes.median(),
    "Shuffled 2.5%": changes.quantile(0.025),
    "Shuffled 97.5%": changes.quantile(0.975),
    "Shuffles ≥ observed change": extreme_changes,
    "Total shuffles": B,
    "Increase p (upper tail)": change_p,
    "Monte Carlo SE": np.sqrt(change_p * (1-change_p) / B),
}], index=["After − before"])

}))

3. Separate count tests at each visit¶

For context, we can ask whether the observed total count at either visit is unusually large. These are secondary diagnostics, distinct from the change test above. Using the same 9,999 assignments, compare each visit's count with its observed count:

$$p_{\mathrm{count},v} =\frac{1+\#\{C_{v,b}\ge C_{v,\mathrm{observed}}\}}{9999+1}.$$

The site-level limma test remains two-sided; these count tests are upper-tailed. They ask about an excess of red sites. The two visit-specific p-values are shown separately, without an across-visit adjustment.

The histograms show shuffled counts with a red line at each observed count. Dark bars are the upper tails used for the p-values. Their middle 95% ranges describe shuffled counts, not confidence intervals for diet effects. A few paired counts are also shown.

B = len(null_counts)
assert B == run["repetitions"]
saved_count_test = pd.read_csv(OUT / "count_test_summary.csv").set_index("time")
count_rows = []
for time in TIMES:
    observed_count = int(summary.loc[time, "highlighted"])
    # Keep limma p-values inside the red-site rule. Only the total count is tested here.
    extreme = int((null_counts[time] >= observed_count).sum())
    count_p = (1 + extreme) / (B + 1)
    assert extreme == saved_count_test.loc[time, "shuffles_ge_observed"]
    assert np.isclose(count_p, saved_count_test.loc[time, "count_p_upper"])
    count_rows.append({
        "Visit": time.title(),
        "Observed red sites": observed_count,
        "Shuffle median": int(null_counts[time].median()),
        "Shuffled 2.5%": null_counts[time].quantile(0.025),
        "Shuffled 97.5%": null_counts[time].quantile(0.975),
        "Shuffles ≥ observed": extreme,
        "Count p (upper tail)": count_p,
        "Monte Carlo SE": np.sqrt(count_p * (1 - count_p) / B),
    })
count_results = pd.DataFrame(count_rows).set_index("Visit")

}))

5. What “fold change” means in this reconstruction¶

A beta value $β$ describes methylation on a scale from 0 to 1. Our reconstruction uses the transformed value

$$M=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\right), \qquad \Delta M=\overline M_{\mathrm{vegan}}-\overline M_{\mathrm{meat\! -\! rich}}.$$

The saved limma column logFC contains $\Delta M$. Consequently, $2^{\Delta M}$ is the ratio of geometric mean methylation odds between the two groups. An effect of 0.5 corresponds to an odds ratio of $\sqrt{2}\approx1.414$. It is not a 50-percentage-point change, nor a ratio of arithmetic mean beta values. The author confirmed M-value input. We derive M-values from the public processed beta matrix; the original M-value matrix has not been supplied.

The author confirmed the initial four-group-by-time-mean model. Our R fit includes all five supplied contrasts; we use vegan minus meat-rich at each visit for Figure 1B. The model has 92 residual degrees of freedom and no participant blocking. limma moderates the site variances by borrowing information across CpGs, making individual variance estimates less unstable. Its parametric p-values then use a moderated t reference distribution. This is not the ordinary Welch t-test.

The two visits are correlated within a person. The original limma model does not explicitly model that correlation; the participant shuffles preserve the pairs. Both visit-specific contrasts are between-group comparisons. They do not directly test whether the two groups changed differently from baseline.

Randomization-block restrictions concern which diet reassignments are allowed. They do not add block covariates to this model and are distinct from modeling within-person correlation using duplicateCorrelation.

6. Volcano plots: observed groups and one shuffled grouping¶

Each point is one CpG. The horizontal coordinate is the fitted mean M-value difference; the vertical coordinate is $-\log_{10}(p^{\mathrm{limma}})$. Dashed lines show the same thresholds in all four panels, and red points meet both.

  • Top row: the observed grouping, giving 158 red sites before and 182 after.
  • Bottom row: one within-block participant reassignment from the example seed shown below. Each block retains its observed diet counts. The same reassignment is applied to both visits and every CpG. The same R/limma script refits the model and variance moderation.

Both fitted effects and limma p-values change when the groups are reassigned. The example is the first assignment generated by its specified seed, chosen before fitting. Its saved p-values and fitted effects are checked against the red-site counts. The example seed can be changed independently of the full count-test seed.

The p-values on the vertical axes are the limma p-values fitted within each displayed grouping. The bottom row provides a visual sanity check. The change-test histogram in section 2 uses all 9,999 assignments to assess the increase of +24. The separate visit-specific count diagnostics are in section 3. Both rows use the corrected visit labels for donors 5 and 8. The earlier example counts and figures remain in the archived unrestricted results.

7. What the blocked change test establishes¶

The reconstructed increase is 182 − 158 = +24 red sites. Of 9,999 within-block participant shuffles, 1,619 give an increase of at least +24, yielding an upper-tail permutation p-value of 0.1620 with the +1 correction. The shuffled median is +0; the middle 95% range is -101.05 to +78.00. The approximate Monte Carlo standard error is 0.0037.

The increase is not unusual under this conditional within-block procedure. The preceding corrected-visits unrestricted result was p = 0.1881; the original deposited-visits result was p = 0.2630 for +18. The current fit uses the corrected visits, verified diets and new block restrictions. The same seed samples different assignments under the new rules.

Each difference uses paired counts from one assignment. A net increase of 24 can involve sites entering and leaving the red set. This test does not identify individual CpG effects or directly test their diet-by-time interactions. The statistic and upper-tail direction were chosen during exploratory review. A large p-value cannot establish absence of a diet effect or equivalence of the diets.

Diet meaning and all participant assignments and blocks are now verified against the author's table. The original input M-values, site-level result identities, individual sex corrections and the full subset-selection mechanism remain unverified. This added test does not show that published individual-CpG p-values are incorrect. The paper's normalization, probe filtering and other outcomes are outside this analysis.

The blocked audit checks the supplied allocations, four visit changes, original input hashes, all restrictions, summary values and independent R fits. Historical audits retain their original scope.

Numerical verification and Monte Carlo stability

All 24 automated tests pass, including comparisons with R/limma, participant alignment, visit-correction integrity, within-block count preservation, the fixed singleton, invalid allocation rejection, rejection of changed sample/block inputs and the unchanged historical unrestricted RNG sequence.

The blocked audit reproduces 11 full-data R fits using independent factorial model coding and assignments reconstructed directly from IDs. Every red-site count agrees. The largest observed absolute statistic discrepancy is 2.74e-13. The invariance audit checks explicit residual calculations, group/visit/order symmetries and sample distances.

A separate 9,999-shuffle run with seed 70901 gives p = 0.1617, compared with 0.1620 for seed 70899. Both use the same block restrictions. The verification run is reported separately and is not pooled with the primary run. The table below independently recalculates both upper tails and the historical results.

The 6 November review replayed all 9,999 fitted shuffles and recovered every saved count pair exactly. Its full replay record confirms p = 0.1620. The observed overlap is 85 shared, 73 before-only and 97 after-only red sites, providing additional agreement with the published totals.

import hashlib

# Independently recompute each tail from its own paired rows.
check_run = json.loads((ROOT / "results/blocked_randomization/audit/independent_seed_summary.json").read_text())
check_counts = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "results/blocked_randomization/audit/independent_seed_counts.csv")
assert check_run["seed"] != run["seed"]
assert check_run["annotation_scenario"] == run["annotation_scenario"]
assert check_run["samples_sha256"] == run["samples_sha256"]
assert check_run["block_file_sha256"] == run["block_file_sha256"]
assert check_run["permutation_scheme"] == run["permutation_scheme"]
assert len(check_counts) == check_run["repetitions"]
assert hashlib.sha256((OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv").read_bytes()).hexdigest() == check_run["original_count_sha256"]
observed_change = int(summary.loc["after", "highlighted"] - summary.loc["before", "highlighted"])
stability = []
for label, seed, pairs in [
    ("Within blocks: primary", run["seed"], pd.read_csv(OUT / "permutation_null_counts.csv")),
    ("Within blocks: verification", check_run["seed"], check_counts),
]:
    count = int(((pairs.after - pairs.before) >= observed_change).sum())
    p = (count + 1) / (len(pairs) + 1)
    if label == "Within blocks: verification":
        assert count == check_run["shuffles_ge_observed_change"]
        assert np.isclose(p, check_run["p_upper"])
    stability.append({"Run": label, "Seed": seed, "Shuffles": len(pairs),
                      "Changes ≥ observed": count, "Upper-tail p": p,
                      "Monte Carlo SE": np.sqrt(p * (1-p) / len(pairs))})
display(pd.DataFrame(stability).set_index("Run").style.format({
    "Upper-tail p": "{:.4f}", "Monte Carlo SE": "{:.4f}"}))

# The old p-value uses its own +18 statistic and old fitted counts.
old_counts = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "results/diet_code/permutation_null_counts.csv")
old_change = int(archived_summary.loc["after", "highlighted"] - archived_summary.loc["before", "highlighted"])
old_extreme = int(((old_counts.after - old_counts.before) >= old_change).sum())
old_p = (old_extreme + 1) / (len(old_counts) + 1)
comparison_rows = []
for label, folder in [
    ("Original visits, unrestricted", ROOT / "results/diet_code"),
    ("Corrected visits, unrestricted", ROOT / "results/corrected_visits/diet_code"),
    ("Corrected visits, within blocks", OUT),
]:
    observed = pd.read_csv(folder / "limma_summary.csv").set_index("time")
    pairs = pd.read_csv(folder / "permutation_null_counts.csv")
    before, after = (int(observed.loc[t, "highlighted"]) for t in TIMES)
    extreme = int(((pairs.after-pairs.before) >= after-before).sum())
    comparison_rows.append({"Scenario": label, "Before": before, "After": after,
                            "Change": after-before, "Upper-tail p": (extreme+1)/(len(pairs)+1)})
comparison = pd.DataFrame(comparison_rows).set_index("Scenario")
display(Markdown("**Historical comparison: each row uses its own observations and permutation distribution.**"))
display(comparison.style.format({"Upper-tail p": "{:.4f}"}))

full_replay = json.loads((ROOT / "results/blocked_randomization/audit/full_replay_summary.json").read_text())
assert full_replay["all_paired_counts_equal"]
assert full_replay["seed"] == run["seed"] and full_replay["repetitions"] == B
assert full_replay["original_count_sha256"] == check_run["original_count_sha256"]
assert full_replay["samples_sha256"] == run["samples_sha256"]
assert full_replay["block_file_sha256"] == run["block_file_sha256"]
assert np.isclose(full_replay["p_upper"], change_p)

8. Sensitivity to pooling the visits in the limma model¶

The author-confirmed four-cell model pools residual variance across visits. A separate fit at each visit provides an alternative model comparison. Both rows below use the same verified diet assignments and corrected visits. The permutation test uses the four-cell model throughout.

Fits based on the conflicting deposited named-diet field remain archived under results/corrected_visits/diet_named/. Those assignments disagree with the author's verified table, so they are excluded from the current diet comparison. The later age/sex-adjusted model with participant correlation is outside this analysis.

pooled = pd.read_csv(OUT / "limma_summary.csv").set_index("time")
separate = pd.read_csv(OUT / "separate_time_sensitivity.csv").set_index("time")
sensitivity = []
for model, table, indices in [("Four cell means", pooled, TIMES),
                              ("Separate visits", separate, (0, 1))]:
    sensitivity.append({"Model": model,
        "Before highlighted": int(table.loc[indices[0], "highlighted"]),
        "After highlighted": int(table.loc[indices[1], "highlighted"]),
        "Before BH < 0.05": int(table.loc[indices[0], "bh_below_005"]),
        "After BH < 0.05": int(table.loc[indices[1], "bh_below_005"])})
display(pd.DataFrame(sensitivity).set_index("Model"))

9. Inspect an individual CpG from the limma analysis¶

This optional example shows the measurements behind one point in the observed volcano plots. Set SITE below to a CpG ID and rerun the example. With SITE = None, we select the red follow-up site with the smallest limma p-value. This is a descriptive selection after inspecting the results, not independent confirmation of an effect.

The table shows the fitted M-value difference, original raw limma p-value, and its Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment over all CpGs at that visit. No site in the numeric grouping has a BH-adjusted p-value below 0.05. Red sites follow the figure's raw-p and effect rule; they are not genome-wide discoveries after multiple-testing correction.

The plots show each participant's measured beta values and group means. Each person appears in both panels. These beta means are descriptive; the fitted effect uses M-values.

columns = ["cpg", "logFC", "t", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val"]
results = {
    time: pd.read_csv(OUT / f"{time}_limma.csv.gz", usecols=columns).set_index("cpg")
    for time in TIMES
}
for time, table in results.items():
    assert len(table) == audit["matrix_shape"][0] and table.index.is_unique
    assert np.isfinite(table.to_numpy()).all()
    for pcol in ("P.Value", "adj.P.Val"):
        assert table[pcol].between(0, 1).all()
    table["highlighted"] = (table.logFC.abs() > EFFECT_CUTOFF) & (table["P.Value"] < ALPHA)
    assert int(table.highlighted.sum()) == summary.loc[time, "highlighted"]

SITE = None  # Replace with an ID such as "cg14817997" to inspect another site.
if SITE is None:
    candidates = results["after"].loc[results["after"].highlighted, "P.Value"]
    SITE = candidates.idxmin() if len(candidates) else results["after"]["P.Value"].idxmin()
if not all(SITE in table.index for table in results.values()):
    raise KeyError(f"CpG {SITE!r} is absent from the result tables")

display(Markdown(f"**Selected CpG: `{SITE}`**"))
site_table = pd.DataFrame({time.title(): table.loc[SITE, [
    "logFC", "P.Value", "adj.P.Val", "highlighted"
]] for time, table in results.items()}).T.rename(columns={
    "logFC": "ΔM (vegan − meat-rich)", "P.Value": "limma raw p", "adj.P.Val": "limma BH-adjusted p",
    "highlighted": "Red under original rule",
})
display(site_table)

beta_path = ROOT / "data/processed/beta.bin"
if beta_path.exists():
    shape = tuple(audit["matrix_shape"])
    assert beta_path.stat().st_size == np.prod(shape) * 8
    # Check the explicit CpG ordering before looking up any beta values.
    cpg_ids = pd.Index((ROOT / "data/processed/cpg_ids.txt").read_text().splitlines())
    assert cpg_ids.equals(results["before"].index) and cpg_ids.equals(results["after"].index)
    row = cpg_ids.get_loc(SITE)
    beta = np.memmap(beta_path, dtype="<f8", mode="r", shape=shape)
    observed = samples.copy()
    observed["beta"] = np.array(beta[row])
    del beta
    jitter_rng = np.random.default_rng(70899)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
    for time, ax in enumerate(axes):
        for x, (group, color) in enumerate((("0", "#208c72"), ("1", "#cc7847"))):
            values = observed.loc[(observed.time == time) & (observed.diet_code == group), "beta"]
            ax.scatter(x + jitter_rng.uniform(-0.09, 0.09, len(values)), values,
                       color=color, s=25, alpha=0.8)
            ax.hlines(values.mean(), x-0.18, x+0.18, color="black", lw=2)
        ax.set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=["Vegan", "Meat-rich"],
               xlim=(-0.5, 1.5), ylim=(0, 1), title=TIMES[time].title(), ylabel="Beta value")
    fig.suptitle(f"{SITE} — measured beta values; black lines are group means")
    plt.show()
else:
    display(Markdown("The prepared beta matrix is unavailable. The saved per-site test results above remain viewable; run `make prepare` to enable the participant plots."))

Rerun, explore, and trace the sources¶

  • Explore: change SITE in section 9, or filter the per-CpG results tables.
  • Recompute summaries: run make change-test and make count-test from saved counts.
  • Change the illustrative shuffle: run make plots EXAMPLE_SEED=70900, then make execute-notebook.
  • Refresh this notebook and HTML: run make execute-notebook.
  • Repeat the full analysis: follow the README: make prepare, make limma, make permutation PERMUTATIONS=9999 SEED=70899, then make plots.
  • Extract the original workbook again, if available locally: make randomization. The committed allocation CSV suffices for reproduction without the workbook.
  • Repeat validation: run make test and make audit. The current audit validates all block restrictions and independent full-data R fits. Historical audit records remain in their original folders.
  • Repeat the separate Monte Carlo check: OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=4 OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 .venv/bin/python scripts/audit_results.py --scenario blocked_randomization --independent-seed 70901.
  • Implementation: limma model, joint shuffles, allocation restrictions, block audit, change test.

Analysis commands default to blocked_randomization. The explicit scenarios corrected_visits and deposited reproduce historical unrestricted analyses and can overwrite their generated outputs. This notebook always reads the current blocked run.

Primary sources: paper, public dataset, limma guide, Monte Carlo permutation p-values, exchangeability, and author-supplied allocation provenance.
